etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English tender, tendere, from Anglo-Norman tendre, Old French tendre, from Latin tener, tenerum (“soft, delicate”).
senses: Sensitive or painful to the touch.
Easily bruised or injured; not firm or hard; delicate.
The inner flight muscle (pectoralis minor) of poultry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: From Middle English tender, tendur, tendir, tendre, from the adjective (see above).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
paragraphs: From Middle English tendren, from the adjective (see above).
senses: (now rare) To make tender or delicate; to weaken.
(archaic) To feel tenderly towards; to regard fondly or with consideration.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
paragraphs: From tend +‎ -er. Compare attender (“one who attends”).
senses: (rail transport) A specialized rail wagon hauled behind a steam engine to carry fuel and water.
(nautical) A naval ship that functions as a mobile base for other ships.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
paragraphs: From Middle English tendren, from Old French tendre (“stretch out”).
senses: Anything which is offered, proffered, put forth or bid with the expectation of a response, answer, or reply.
To offer a payment, as at sales or auctions; to bid.
